cards.back: The method that runs is chosen from the object's actual type at runtime, not the reference type
cards.extra: The compiler only checks that the method exists on the declared type; the JVM dispatches to the override. It is what makes polymorphism work.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::15 Static vs Dynamic Binding
cards.example:
class Instrument { void play() { } }
class Piano extends Instrument { void play() { System.out.println("piano"); } }
class Demo { void run() { Instrument i = new Piano(); i.play(); } }  // piano: actual type at runtime

cards.front: What does upcasting buy you in tune(Instrument i)?
cards.back: One method serves every Instrument subtype, including ones written later
cards.extra: The alternative is a type-specific method per subclass, and the compiler will not warn you when you forget one. Upcasting is what makes the code extensible.
cards.example:
class Instrument { }
class Violin extends Instrument { }
class Band { void tune(Instrument i) { } void go() { tune(new Violin()); } }  // one method for all subtypes, even future ones

cards.back: No — they are statically bound and cannot be overridden
cards.extra: A subclass method with the same name is a different method entirely. Calling it through a base reference runs the base version.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::15 Static vs Dynamic Binding
cards.example:
class Base { private void hint() { } void call() { hint(); } }
class Sub extends Base { private void hint() { } }  // not an override: call() still runs Base.hint()
class Demo { void run() { new Sub().call(); } }

cards.back: No — field access is resolved at compile time from the reference type
cards.extra: Two classes can declare the same field name and both exist in the object; which one you see depends on the static type of the reference.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::15 Static vs Dynamic Binding
cards.example:
class Base { int v = 1; }
class Sub extends Base { int v = 2; }
class Demo { void run() { Base r = new Sub(); System.out.println(r.v); } }  // 1: field from reference type

cards.back: No — they belong to the class, so the reference type decides
cards.extra: Static methods are not overridden, only hidden. Calling one through an instance is legal but misleading.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::15 Static vs Dynamic Binding
cards.example:
class Base { static void who() { System.out.println("Base"); } }
class Sub extends Base { static void who() { System.out.println("Sub"); } }
class Demo { void run() { Base r = new Sub(); r.who(); } }  // Base: reference type decides

cards.front: What is the design payoff of polymorphism?
cards.back: New code can be added without modifying the code that uses the base type
cards.extra: The book frames it as decoupling types: the caller knows the base contract only, so a new subclass slots in with no edits — the open/closed principle.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::15 Static vs Dynamic Binding
cards.example:
class Shape { void draw() { } }
class Circle extends Shape { void draw() { System.out.println("circle"); } }
class Renderer { void drawAll(Shape[] xs) { for (Shape s : xs) s.draw(); } }  // no edit needed for new shapes
